mappings.note: Unlike poles attract, like poles repel. The central phenomenon of the chapter stated as a rule, LO-32; nothing is being sorted, so not LO-29.
Materials attracted to a magnet are called magnetic materials. Naming a class defined by an observable property, LO-29.
True or false: a magnet can be broken to obtain a single pole. Explaining why poles always come in pairs, LO-32.
True or false on like poles repelling. Same phenomenon as the preceding pair of items; this row duplicates item 3's stem with its answer appended.
Completes the N-N, N-S, S-N, S-S interaction table. Applying the attraction and repulsion rule across all four cases, LO-32.
Place the magnet under the paper, tap, and observe where the filings gather. A hands-on investigation with observations to be made, LO-30.
Push the suspended magnet, wait, and check it rests on the same line. LO-30 names 'whether a freely suspended magnet aligns in a particular direction' as its own example.
Records predictions and observations in the magnetic-materials table. LO-30 for recording observations during the activity, LO-29 for the magnetic/non-magnetic sorting that results.
Repeat the compass test with the South pole and look for a difference. A conducted investigation varying one factor, LO-30.
Substitute cardboard, plastic and glass for the wood between magnet and compass. An investigation across several materials, LO-30.
Spin the floating cork repeatedly and check the needle always settles the same way. Repeated trials of the alignment investigation, LO-30.
Bring the other end of magnet B to the same end of A and say what the observations suggest. An investigation whose inference the student must draw, LO-30.
Stem is a stray heading, but the answer explains that the most U-clips cling at the ends and fewest at the middle because strength is concentrated at the poles. Explaining the phenomenon, LO-32.
Identify which two of three identical bars are magnets with nothing else to hand. The student must devise the repulsion test, which is planning an investigation, LO-30.
Find an unmarked magnet's poles using a marked one. A procedure to be designed and run, LO-30.
Locate the North pole WITHOUT another magnet, by free suspension. LO-30's stated example, and the constraint is what forces that method.
Infer the polarity of Earth's magnetic poles from which way a compass points. Relating an observed phenomenon to its cause, LO-31.
The mechanic's steel screws keep dropping -- magnetise the screwdriver. Applying the chapter's learning to a real task, LO-36.
Why ring magnet X will not descend, and how to close the gap. The floating is explained by like-pole repulsion balancing weight -- a phenomenon related to its cause, LO-31.
Deduce the polarity at five ends of three arranged magnets from one given pole. Applying the attraction rule and the pairing of poles, LO-32.
The naturally occurring magnetic rock is lodestone. Identifying a material by name and property, LO-27.
Which is an artificial magnet. Sorting magnets into natural and man-made, LO-29.
Why iron, nickel and cobalt are called magnetic materials. The defining property of a class, LO-29.
What non-magnetic materials are. The complementary class, LO-29.
Where iron filings stick on a bar magnet. Recall of Activity 4.2's observed result, LO-30.
The ends where the force is strongest are the poles. Identifying a part of the magnet by an observable feature, LO-27.
Breaking a magnet leaves each piece with both poles. Explaining why poles cannot be isolated, LO-32.
A freely suspended bar magnet settles North-South. LO-30's own worked example.
The end pointing to geographic north is the north-seeking pole. Naming a pole from its observable behaviour, LO-27.
The device with a freely rotating magnetised needle is a compass. LO-36 names 'using a compass needle to find directions' explicitly.
WHY a suspended magnet rests North-South -- because Earth is itself a magnet. The cause is what is marked, LO-31, not the observation, which is LO-30.
Magnetise a sewing needle by stroking it with one pole. The step that makes the homemade compass work, so LO-35, construct from surrounding materials and explain the working.
North near South gives attraction. The pole-interaction phenomenon, LO-32.
North near North gives repulsion. The other half of the same phenomenon, LO-32.
Repulsion is the sure test for a magnet. LO-30 for the test and LO-28 because the whole point is telling a magnet apart from a merely magnetic material, which attraction cannot do.
The matsya-yantra, a magnetised fish floating in oil. An applied direction-finding device, LO-36.
Reshma navigating under overcast sky with a freely rotating needle. Using a compass to find directions, LO-36's own example.
Wood is the non-magnetic one among iron, nickel and cobalt. Sorting materials by magnetic response, LO-29.
Assertion-reason where the reason is Earth's magnetic field. The causal link is what the item marks, LO-31.

Which statements about poles hold -- the correct one is that the ends of strongest attraction are the poles. Identification of the poles by observable feature, LO-27. The stem retains only one of the three numbered statements.
Why Activity 4.1 asks for a prediction before the test -- to form a hypothesis. Method of investigation, LO-30.
Paper between magnet and compass leaves the deflection unchanged. Explaining that magnetic force passes through non-magnetic material, LO-32; item 10 was the activity, this is its explanation.
Man-made magnets are artificial magnets. The natural/artificial classification, LO-29.
Storing magnets in pairs with unlike poles adjacent, wood between and iron keepers across. A practical handling rule, LO-36.
An iron bar is attracted by both poles, whereas a second magnet can also be repelled. An explicit differentiation of two materials by their behaviour, LO-28.
Which action is NOT safe for magnets -- heating them. Care of equipment in practice, LO-36.
Two magnet-carrying toy cars push apart, so like poles face each other. Reading the phenomenon back to the pole rule, LO-32; the car is only the vehicle, so not LO-35.
Assertion-reason: the compass needle is itself a magnet, which is why it deflects. The deflection is related to its cause, LO-31.
Which listed items a magnet attracts -- steel and cobalt yes, plastic no. Sorting materials by magnetic response, LO-29. The stem preserves only the last of the three numbered items.

A recycling plant separating iron and steel from mixed waste. LO-36 for the applied use of magnetic attraction and LO-37 because the application is waste recovery, which LO-37 covers as reducing waste generation.
Sailors navigated by magnetic compass when stars were hidden. Applied direction-finding, LO-36.
Tell a bar magnet from an identical iron bar with nothing else. The discriminating property is repulsion, so a differentiation on behaviour, LO-28.
The U-shape among common artificial magnet shapes. Identification by appearance, LO-27.
The needle-and-cork compass built in Activity 4.4 settles North-South. A model made from everyday materials whose working must be explained, LO-35.
Maximum filings at the poles, very few in the middle. Explaining the uneven distribution of magnetic force, LO-32.
Which everyday object does NOT carry a magnet. Recognising magnets in daily objects, LO-36.
If A's North attracts an end of B, that end is South. Deduction from the attraction rule, LO-32.
Assertion-reason with a false reason: plastic is NOT attracted. Tests the magnetic/non-magnetic classification, LO-29.

Which statements hold -- a magnet has two poles, strength is greatest at the poles, and cutting leaves both poles. Explaining the pole phenomena, LO-32. Only one of the three numbered statements survives in the stem.
A paperclip jumps without contact, showing magnetic force acts at a distance. Explaining the phenomenon, LO-32.
